stem: A right rectangular prism has a base area of \(16t\) square centimeters (cm²). The length of the base of the rectangular prism is \(\frac{8}{3}\) cm, and the height of the rectangular prism is 9 cm. Which expression represents the surface area, in cm², of the right rectangular prism?
whyCorrect: Get the missing width first: the base area is length times width, so \(w = 16t \div \frac{8}{3} = 6t\). Surface area is two bases plus the four side faces: \(2(16t) + 2\left(\frac{8}{3}\cdot 9\right) + 2(6t \cdot 9) = 32t + 48 + 108t\), which is \(140t + 48\).

whyWrong.A: This treats the base as a square of side \(\frac{8}{3}\), so the side faces come out as \(4\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)(9) = 96\) and the two \(6t \times 9\) faces are lost.
whyWrong.C: This multiplies instead of divides when finding the width: \(16t \cdot \frac{8}{3} = \frac{128t}{3}\) gives side faces of \(768t + 48\), and \(768t + 32t = 800t\).
whyWrong.D: \(144t\) is the volume, base area times height \(16t \cdot 9\), not the surface area.

stem: A cube has an edge length of 82 inches. A solid sphere with a radius of 41 inches is inside the cube, such that the sphere touches the center of each face of the cube. To the nearest cubic inch, what is the volume of the space in the cube not taken up by the sphere?
whyCorrect: The leftover space is the cube's volume minus the sphere's volume. The cube gives \(82^3 = 551{,}368\) and the sphere gives \(\frac{4}{3}\pi(41)^3 \approx 288{,}695.61\). Subtracting, \(551{,}368 - 288{,}695.61 \approx 262{,}672\).

whyWrong.B: This is the volume the sphere itself occupies, not the space left over around it.
whyWrong.C: This subtracts \(\pi r^3\) instead of \(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\); dropping the \(\frac{4}{3}\) makes the sphere too small and the leftover space too big.
whyWrong.D: This subtracts the area of a circle, \(\pi(41)^2 \approx 5{,}281\), instead of the volume of a sphere.

stem: In triangle PQR, the measure of angle P is \((3x + 5)^\circ\), the measure of angle Q is \((2x + 9)^\circ\), and the measure of angle R is \((4y + 5)^\circ\). If side QR is extended through point R to point S and the measure of angle PRS is \((x + y)^\circ\), what is the value of \(x + y\)?
whyCorrect: Angle PRS is the exterior angle at R, so it equals the sum of the two remote interior angles: \(x + y = (3x+5) + (2x+9) = 5x + 14\). It is also supplementary to angle R, so \((x+y) + (4y+5) = 180\). The first equation gives \(y = 4x + 14\); substituting into \(x + 5y = 175\) gives \(21x = 105\), so \(x = 5\) and \(y = 34\), and \(x + y = 39\). (Check: the angles are 20°, 19° and 141°, which sum to 180°.)

stem:
Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
In the given figure, NP is the diameter of semicircle O. Angles Q, R, and S are right angles, and point P is the midpoint of NQ. If PQ = 52 feet and NS = 18 feet, the area of the figure can be expressed as \(a\pi + b\) square feet, where a and b are integers. What is the value of \(a - b\)?
whyCorrect: Because P is the midpoint of NQ, \(NP = PQ = 52\), so \(NQ = 104\) and the semicircle has radius 26. The figure is the rectangle NQRS plus the semicircle: rectangle \(= 104 \cdot 18 = 1872\), semicircle \(= \frac{1}{2}\pi(26)^2 = 338\pi\). So \(a = 338\), \(b = 1872\), and \(a - b = -1534\). The trap is using 52 as the diameter instead of half of NQ.
note: Figure: rectangle NQRS with N top-left, Q top-right, R bottom-right, S bottom-left; a semicircle with centre O sits on top of side NQ with diameter NP, P lying between O and Q on NQ. Answer is negative because b is much larger than a.

stem: Point M lies on a unit circle in the xy-plane and has coordinates \((1, 0)\). Point C is the center of the circle at \((0, 0)\). Point N also lies on the unit circle, and the measure of angle MCN is \(\frac{385\pi}{6}\) radians. If the coordinates of point N are \((p, q)\), where p and q are constants, what is the value of q?
whyCorrect: Strip off whole turns first. \(\frac{385\pi}{6} = \frac{384\pi}{6} + \frac{\pi}{6} = 64\pi + \frac{\pi}{6}\), and \(64\pi\) is 32 complete revolutions, so N sits where the angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) puts it. On the unit circle the coordinates are \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\), so \(q = \sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}\).

whyWrong.A: This is \(\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\) — it comes from rotating clockwise, or from subtracting the leftover \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) from a full turn instead of adding it.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) is \(\cos\frac{\pi}{6}\), which is p, the x-coordinate, not q.
whyWrong.C: This is the x-coordinate with a sign error: it uses cosine instead of sine and places the point in the wrong quadrant.

note: The standard counterclockwise convention is assumed; a clockwise reading of the same angle would put N at -1/2.

stem: In the figure above, AB = AD, BC = CD, BE = 4, BC = 8, and AC = 12. What is the area of triangle ABD?
whyCorrect: ABCD is a kite, so diagonal AC is the perpendicular bisector of BD: the diagonals meet at right angles at E and \(BD = 2(BE) = 8\). Right triangle BEC gives \(EC = \sqrt{8^2 - 4^2} = 4\sqrt{3}\), so the height from A is \(AE = AC - EC = 12 - 4\sqrt{3}\). Then the area of ABD is \(\frac{1}{2}(BD)(AE) = \frac{1}{2}(8)(12 - 4\sqrt{3}) = 48 - 16\sqrt{3}\).

whyWrong.A: This is \((BD)(AE)\) with the \(\frac{1}{2}\) of the triangle-area formula left out.
whyWrong.C: This uses \(BE = 4\) as the whole base instead of \(BD = 8\); E is the midpoint of BD, so the base is twice BE.
whyWrong.D: \(12 - 4\sqrt{3}\) is AE itself, the height of the triangle, not its area.

note: Figure: kite ABCD with A at the left vertex, C at the right vertex, B above and D below; diagonals AC and BD cross at E.

stem: A futuristic football is built from two right circular cones and a right circular cylinder with internal measurements represented by the figure above. Of the following, which is closest to the volume of the football, in cubic inches?
whyCorrect: The solid is one cylinder plus two identical cones, all sharing the radius 3 in. The cylinder holds \(\pi(3)^2(6) = 54\pi\); each cone holds \(\frac{1}{3}\pi(3)^2(3) = 9\pi\), so the two together add \(18\pi\). The total is \(72\pi \approx 226.2\) cubic inches.

whyWrong.A: \(18\pi \approx 56.5\) is the two cones alone, with the cylinder body left out.
whyWrong.B: \(54\pi \approx 169.6\) is the cylinder alone, with both pointed ends left out.
whyWrong.C: \(63\pi \approx 197.9\) counts the cylinder and only one cone; the football has a cone at each end.

note: Figure: a vertical cylinder of height 6 in with a cone attached at each end; the label on the top face is a radius of 3 in, and each cone has height 3 in.

stem:
Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
In the figure, \(\angle ABD = w^\circ\), \(\angle CAD = z^\circ\), and \(\cos w = \frac{9}{41}\). What is the value of \(\tan z\)?
whyCorrect: The altitude from the right angle splits the triangle into two triangles similar to the original, and the quick consequence is \(z = w\): in right triangle ABD, \(\angle BAD = 90^\circ - w\), and since \(\angle BAC = 90^\circ\), \(z = 90^\circ - \angle BAD = w\). From \(\cos w = \frac{9}{41}\), the triangle is a 9-40-41 right triangle, so \(\sin w = \frac{40}{41}\) and \(\tan z = \tan w = \frac{40}{9}\).
note: Figure: right triangle ABC with the right angle at A (bottom left), B at the top, C at the bottom right; D lies on BC with AD perpendicular to BC.

stem: Identical rectangles X and Y each have an area of \(\frac{49}{5}\) square meters and a perimeter of P meters. If one of the shorter sides of rectangle X is glued to one of the shorter sides of rectangle Y, the resulting rectangle has a perimeter of \(\frac{14}{9}P\) meters. What is the value of P?
whyCorrect: Call the long side L and the short side s, so \(P = 2(L+s)\). Gluing along the short sides makes a \(2L \times s\) rectangle of perimeter \(4L + 2s\), so \(4L + 2s = \frac{14}{9}(2L+2s)\), which simplifies to \(8L = 10s\), i.e. \(L = \frac{5}{4}s\). Substituting into \(Ls = \frac{49}{5}\) gives \(s^2 = \frac{196}{25}\), so \(s = \frac{14}{5}\) and \(L = \frac{7}{2}\), and \(P = 2\left(\frac{7}{2} + \frac{14}{5}\right) = 12.6\).

stem: In the figure above, P and N are the centers of the circles and PN = 6. What is the area of the intersection?
whyCorrect: Each circle passes through the other's center, so both radii equal \(PN = 6\). The common chord subtends a \(120^\circ\) angle at each center, so one circular segment is sector minus triangle: \(\frac{1}{2}(6)^2\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) - \frac{1}{2}(6)^2\sin 120^\circ = 12\pi - 9\sqrt{3}\). The lens is two such segments, one from each circle: \(24\pi - 18\sqrt{3}\).

whyWrong.A: This uses a half circle, \(18\pi\), in place of the \(120^\circ\) sector and then counts only one segment.
whyWrong.B: This doubles the sector correctly but subtracts the triangle only once; each of the two segments has its own triangle to remove.
whyWrong.D: \(36\pi\) is the area of an entire circle, not two \(120^\circ\) sectors; only a third of each circle lies on the sector side of the chord.

note: Figure: two congruent overlapping circles with centres P (left) and N (right), each passing through the other's centre; the shaded lens is their overlap and PN is drawn across it.

stem:
Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
In quadrilateral KLMN shown, KL = 3, LM = 3, KN = 27, and MN = 27. Diagonals KM and LN (not shown) intersect at point G (not shown), where GK = 1 and GM = 1. If the length of diagonal LN is \(\sqrt{p} + \sqrt{w}\), where p and w are integers, what is the value of \(p + w\)?
whyCorrect: Both L and N are equidistant from K and M, so KLMN is a kite and LN is the perpendicular bisector of KM. That makes triangles LGK and NGK right triangles with leg \(GK = 1\): \(LG = \sqrt{3^2 - 1^2} = \sqrt{8}\) and \(NG = \sqrt{27^2 - 1^2} = \sqrt{728}\). Since G lies between L and N, \(LN = \sqrt{8} + \sqrt{728}\), so \(p + w = 736\).
note: Figure: quadrilateral KLMN drawn with M top left, N top right, L at the left and K at the bottom; the diagonals are not drawn.

stem: A hollow steel pipe is in the shape of a right circular cylinder. The steel pipe has an outside diameter of 48 inches, a wall thickness of \(\frac{3}{5}\) inches, and a height of 144 inches. Which of the following is closest to the volume, in cubic inches, of the wall of this steel pipe?
whyCorrect: The wall is the outer cylinder minus the hollow inside. The outer radius is 24 and the inner radius is \(24 - \frac{3}{5} = 23.4\), so the volume is \(\pi\left(24^2 - 23.4^2\right)(144) = \pi(28.44)(144) \approx 12{,}866\) cubic inches. Of the four values offered, only 13,395 is anywhere near that, and the question asks for the closest.

whyWrong.A: Far too small — roughly the size of the ring's cross-sectional area (about 89 square inches) rather than a volume; the 144-inch height was never multiplied in.
whyWrong.B: Also a no-height answer: it is about \(2\pi\) times the thickness times the height, which treats \(\frac{3}{5}\) as the radius of the pipe instead of the thickness of its wall.
whyWrong.C: This drops \(\pi\) and multiplies raw dimensions together; a wall wrapped around a 48-inch-diameter pipe is more than six times this.

note: Exact value is about 12,866 cubic inches; the printed choice 13,395 is roughly 4% high, so the question only works because it asks for the closest value.

stem: In the figure, \(\overline{AC}\) is a diameter of the circle with center O, and AC = 10. Triangle \(\triangle ACB\) is equilateral. The length of BP is n times the length of AO. What is the value of n?
whyCorrect: AO is the radius, 5. Segment BO is the altitude of the equilateral triangle of side 10, so \(BO = \sqrt{10^2 - 5^2} = 5\sqrt{3}\). P lies on the circle along BO, so \(PO = 5\) and \(BP = 5\sqrt{3} - 5\). Dividing by \(AO = 5\) gives \(n = \sqrt{3} - 1\).

whyWrong.A: This mis-simplifies \(\sqrt{75}\) as \(5\sqrt{5}\) instead of \(5\sqrt{3}\) (75 is \(25 \cdot 3\)), and also forgets to cut off the radius.
whyWrong.B: \(\sqrt{3}\) is \(BO \div AO\), the whole altitude. P is on the circle, so the radius \(PO = 5\) still has to be subtracted.
whyWrong.D: This subtracts the radius correctly but carries the same \(\sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{5}\) simplification error.

note: Figure: circle with centre O and horizontal diameter AC; B is above the circle, joined to A and C, and the segment from B to O crosses the circle at the point taken as P. The book's figure does not actually label P.

stem: In the xy-plane, a circle has center D with coordinates \((m, 16)\), where m is a constant. Points E and F lie on the circle. Point E lies on the circle and has coordinates \((m + 4\sqrt{10}, 34)\), and point F has coordinates \((n, 16)\), where n is a constant greater than m. What is the area, in square units, of triangle DEF?
whyCorrect: Get the radius from D to E: \(r = \sqrt{(4\sqrt{10})^2 + (34-16)^2} = \sqrt{160 + 324} = 22\). F has the same y-coordinate as the center, so DF is a horizontal radius of length 22 — use it as the base. The height is the vertical distance from E to the line \(y = 16\), which is \(34 - 16 = 18\). Area \(= \frac{1}{2}(22)(18) = 198\).

whyWrong.B: This uses the horizontal offset \(4\sqrt{10}\) as the base, multiplies by the height 18, and omits the \(\frac{1}{2}\).
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{1}{2}(22)(22)\) — it uses the radius as the height. The height is the vertical drop from E to the base line, which is 18, not 22.
whyWrong.D: The \(\sqrt{10}\) should disappear once the radius is computed; keeping it means the coordinate \(4\sqrt{10}\) was used where the vertical distance 18 belongs.

stem:
AreaPerimeter
Rectangle A2,450490
Rectangle B9,800n
The table gives the areas (square inches) and perimeters (inches) of two similar rectangles, where n is a constant. What is the value of n?
whyCorrect: For similar figures, areas scale by the square of the length ratio while perimeters scale by the ratio itself. Here \(\frac{9800}{2450} = 4\), so the length ratio is \(\sqrt{4} = 2\). The perimeter therefore doubles: \(n = 2(490) = 980\).

whyWrong.B: This applies the area ratio 4 directly to the perimeter. Perimeter is a length, so it scales by 2, not by 4.
whyWrong.C: This uses \(2^3 = 8\), the volume scale factor. These are flat rectangles, so nothing here is cubed.
whyWrong.D: This multiplies the perimeter by 10, which matches no ratio in the problem; \(\sqrt{4} = 2\), not 10.

stem: In the figure above, what is the length of NQ?
whyCorrect: Triangle MNP is right-angled at N with legs 3 and 4, so \(MP = 5\). The area can be written two ways: \(\frac{1}{2}(3)(4)\) using the legs, or \(\frac{1}{2}(MP)(NQ)\) using the hypotenuse and the altitude to it. Setting them equal gives \(NQ = \frac{3 \cdot 4}{5} = 2.4\).

whyWrong.A: There is no computation here that gives 2.2; it is a near-miss for a student measuring the figure instead of using the area relation.
whyWrong.B: Same trap as A — the altitude is exactly \(\frac{12}{5}\), so a value of 2.3 means the relationship was estimated rather than computed.
whyWrong.D: 2.5 is half the hypotenuse, which is the length of the median from N to MP. NQ is perpendicular to MP, and in a non-isosceles right triangle the altitude and the median are different segments.

note: Figure: triangle MNP with the right angle at N, MN = 3, NP = 4, and Q the foot of the perpendicular from N to MP.

stem: An equilateral triangle is inscribed in a circle with a radius of 8 inches. What is the area of the region that lies within the circle but outside the triangle, in square inches?
whyCorrect: The circle's area is \(\pi(8)^2 = 64\pi\). For an equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle of radius R, the side is \(R\sqrt{3} = 8\sqrt{3}\), so the triangle's area is \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(8\sqrt{3})^2 = 48\sqrt{3}\). (Same result from three central triangles: \(3 \cdot \frac{1}{2}(8)^2\sin 120^\circ\).) The leftover region is \(64\pi - 48\sqrt{3}\).

whyWrong.B: This is half the triangle's area. The triangle's height is \(R + \frac{R}{2} = 12\), not 6 — the center sits two-thirds of the way along each median, not at the midpoint.
whyWrong.C: \(32\sqrt{3}\) comes from a side of \(8\sqrt{2}\), the relation for an inscribed square. For an equilateral triangle the side is \(R\sqrt{3}\).
whyWrong.D: Every term here is a quarter of the correct one, which is what you get by treating 8 as the diameter and using a radius of 4.

note: The stem says to round to the nearest tenth, but all four choices are exact expressions; the rounding instruction is left over from another version of the question.

stem: In triangles PQR and XYZ, angles R and Z each have a measure of 38°. The length of side QR is equal to 11. The length of side YZ is equal to 27.5. Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle PQR is similar to triangle XYZ?

choices.label: B
choices.content: The length of side PR is 14 and the length of side XZ is 35

choices.label: C
choices.content: The measure of angle Q is 49° and the measure of angle Y is 94°

whyCorrect: Sides QR and PR meet at R, and YZ and XZ meet at Z, so this gives two pairs of sides around the known pair of equal angles. The ratios match: \(\frac{27.5}{11} = 2.5\) and \(\frac{35}{14} = 2.5\). Equal included angles with proportional sides around them is SAS similarity.

whyWrong.A: This is a second angle in PQR only. You still know just one angle of XYZ, so there is no second pair of equal angles to work with.
whyWrong.C: Now PQR has angles 38°, 49°, 93° and XYZ has 38°, 94°, 48°. Those sets are different, so this information proves the triangles are not similar.
whyWrong.D: One pair of equal angles plus one pair of sides proves nothing; with only QR and YZ given, the third vertices can be placed to make the triangles any shape you like.

stem:
Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
In the figure shown, point B lies on line segment DF, point E lies on line segment AC, line segments AB and DE intersect at point W, and line segments BC and EF intersect at point X. The measure of \(\angle A\) is 40°, the measure of \(\angle C\) is 60°, the measure of \(\angle D\) is 68°, and the measure of \(\angle FBC\) is 72°. What is the measure, in degrees, of \(\angle AED\)?
whyCorrect: Work down to the angle at B first. In triangle ABC, \(\angle ABC = 180 - 40 - 60 = 80^\circ\), and since D, B, F are collinear, \(\angle DBA = 180 - 80 - 72 = 28^\circ\). Now use triangle DBW: \(\angle DWB = 180 - 68 - 28 = 84^\circ\), and \(\angle AWE\) is vertical to it, so it is also 84°. Finally, in triangle AWE, \(\angle AEW = 180 - 40 - 84 = 56^\circ\), and D lies on ray EW, so \(\angle AED = 56^\circ\).
note: Figure: A, E, C left to right along a horizontal line; D upper left, B top centre, F upper right with D, B, F collinear. Segment AB crosses DE at W and segment BC crosses EF at X.

stem:
In triangle ABC and triangle DEF, sides AB and DE each have a side length of 10 inches, and angles A and D each have an angle measure of 40°. Which of the following additional pieces of information is (are) sufficient to prove whether triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF?
I. The measures of angles B and C are equal.
II. The lengths of sides AC and DF are equal.
III. The lengths of sides BC and EF are equal.

choices.label: A
choices.content: I is sufficient, but II and III are not.

choices.label: B
choices.content: II is sufficient, but I and III are not.

choices.label: C
choices.content: III is sufficient, but I and II are not.

choices.label: D
choices.content: II is sufficient and III is sufficient, but I is not.

whyCorrect: Angle A sits between sides AB and AC, and angle D sits between DE and DF. So statement II completes side-angle-side: \(AB = DE\), \(\angle A = \angle D\), \(AC = DF\), and the triangles must be congruent.

whyWrong.A: Statement I says something about triangle ABC alone (that it is isosceles). It adds no information at all about DEF, so the two triangles can still differ.
whyWrong.C: Statement III gives side-side-angle: the equal angle is not between the two known sides. With a 40° angle that is the ambiguous case — two different triangles can share \(AB = 10\), \(\angle A = 40^\circ\) and the same length BC.
whyWrong.D: This treats III as sufficient. SSA does not prove congruence; only the included-angle version (II) does.

stem: In the figure above, \(\tan B = \frac{3}{4}\). If BC = 15 and DA = 4, what is the length of DE?
whyCorrect: Triangle ABC has its right angle at A, and \(\tan B = \frac{CA}{BA} = \frac{3}{4}\), so it is a 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 3: \(CA = 9\) and \(BA = 12\). Since D lies on BA with \(DA = 4\), \(BD = 12 - 4 = 8\). Triangle BDE is similar to triangle BAC (both right-angled, sharing angle B), so \(DE = \frac{3}{4}(BD) = \frac{3}{4}(8) = 6\).
note: Figure: right triangle with B at the lower left, A at the lower right and the right angle at A, C directly above A; D is on BA and E is on BC with DE perpendicular to BA.

stem:
Volume
Square pyramid A16
Square pyramid B5488
In geometry, a square pyramid is a pyramid that has a square base and four lateral faces. Square Pyramid A is similar to Square Pyramid B. The table gives the volumes, in cubic inches, of the two square pyramids. If the height of Square pyramid A is 8 inches, what is the perimeter of the square base of Square pyramid B, in inches? (Round your answer to the nearest tenth of an inch)
whyCorrect: First get pyramid A's base edge from \(V = \frac{1}{3}s^2h\): \(16 = \frac{1}{3}s^2(8)\) gives \(s^2 = 6\), so \(s = \sqrt{6}\). Volumes of similar solids scale by the cube of the length ratio, and \(\frac{5488}{16} = 343 = 7^3\), so B's edge is \(7\sqrt{6}\). Its perimeter is \(4(7\sqrt{6}) = 28\sqrt{6} \approx 68.6\) inches.

whyWrong.B: \(4\sqrt{6}\) is the perimeter of pyramid A's base; the scale factor of 7 was never applied.
whyWrong.C: This uses 49 as the length ratio. 49 is the ratio of surface areas; lengths scale by \(\sqrt[3]{343} = 7\).
whyWrong.D: \(7\sqrt{6}\) is one edge of B's base. The question asks for the perimeter, which is four edges.

note: The stem asks for a value rounded to the nearest tenth but every choice is an exact radical expression.

stem: A circle has a center A, and points B and C lie on the circle. Line segments BD and CD are tangent to the circle at points B and C, respectively. The measure of angle BDC is 120°. The length of line segment CD is 12 inches. What is the area of the region that is both inside quadrilateral ABDC and outside the circle, in square inches? (Round your answer to the nearest hundredth of a square inch)
whyCorrect: A tangent meets the radius at 90°, so angles ABD and ACD are right angles and \(\angle BAC = 360 - 90 - 90 - 120 = 60^\circ\). Triangle ACD is right-angled at C with \(\angle ADC = 60^\circ\), so the radius is \(r = 12\tan 60^\circ = 12\sqrt{3}\). The kite is two such triangles: \(2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}(12\sqrt{3})(12) = 144\sqrt{3}\). The circle's share inside it is the 60° sector, \(\frac{1}{6}\pi(12\sqrt{3})^2 = 72\pi\), so the region is \(144\sqrt{3} - 72\pi \approx 23.22\).

whyWrong.B: This is one of the two right triangles and half the sector — the quadrilateral ABDC is made of both triangles.
whyWrong.C: The sector here uses \(r = 12\), the tangent length, instead of the radius \(12\sqrt{3}\): \(\frac{1}{6}\pi(12)^2 = 24\pi\).
whyWrong.D: The \(144\) with no \(\sqrt{3}\) comes from multiplying \(12 \times 12\) as if the radius were also 12, and the circular piece does not match that radius either.

note: The stem asks for a value rounded to the nearest hundredth but every choice is an exact expression.

stem:
Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
In the circle shown, point C is the center, and radius PC bisects AB at point Q. The diameter of the circle has a length of 22. Line segment QP has a length of 3. If the length of line segment AQ is equal to \(\sqrt{x}\), what is the value of x?
whyCorrect: A radius that bisects a chord is perpendicular to it, so triangle AQC has a right angle at Q. The radius is \(\frac{22}{2} = 11\), and Q lies on PC with \(QP = 3\), so \(CQ = 11 - 3 = 8\). Since CA is also a radius, \(AQ^2 = 11^2 - 8^2 = 57\), and \(AQ = \sqrt{57}\), so \(x = 57\). The usual slip is using 11 or 3 as the leg instead of \(CQ = 8\).
note: The book prints a plain diagram (circle with centre C, horizontal chord AB, P at the top, Q where PC meets AB); every value needed is stated in the text.

stem: Point Q is the center of the circle. Point A, point B, and point C all lie on the circle. Point D lies on segment AC as shown. Segment BD is perpendicular to segment AC. In the figure shown, AB = 58 and AD = 40. If a point within the figure is selected at random, what is the probability that the point is within the shaded region? (Express your answer as a decimal or fraction, not as a percent.) Round your answer to the nearest thousandth.
whyCorrect: AC passes through the center, so it is a diameter and angle ABC is a right angle. In right triangle ABD, \(BD = \sqrt{58^2 - 40^2} = 42\), and the geometric-mean relation \(AB^2 = AD \cdot AC\) gives \(AC = \frac{3364}{40} = 84.1\), so the radius is 42.05. The circle's area is \(\pi(42.05)^2 \approx 5554.97\) and the triangle's is \(\frac{1}{2}(84.1)(42) = 1766.1\); the shaded part is everything outside the triangle, so the probability is \(\frac{5554.97 - 1766.1}{5554.97} \approx 0.682\).
note: Figure: circle with centre Q; horizontal diameter AC with A at the left and C at the right, B on the upper arc, D on AC with BD perpendicular to AC. Everything inside the circle except triangle ABC is shaded.

stem: In circle O, there are two diameters, AC and BD. The circumference of the circle is \(96\pi\) and arc AB is three times the length of arc AD. What is the length of arc BC?
whyCorrect: Two diameters cut the circle into four arcs, and vertical angles make opposite arcs equal: arc AB = arc CD and arc BC = arc AD. Let arc AD = t, so arc AB = 3t and the four arcs total \(3t + t + 3t + t = 8t = 96\pi\). So \(t = 12\pi\), and arc BC = arc AD = \(12\pi\).

whyWrong.B: \(24\pi\) is a quarter of the circumference — the answer if the two diameters were perpendicular. Here the arcs are in a 3:1 ratio, so they are not all equal.
whyWrong.C: \(36\pi\) is the length of arc AB (that is, \(3t\)), not arc BC.
whyWrong.D: \(48\pi\) is half the circumference, the arc from A all the way to C along one side.

stem: The measure of angle BDC, in radians, is equal to \(\frac{a\pi}{b}\) where a and b are positive integer constants. What is the smallest possible value of \(a + b\)?
whyCorrect: With D at the center, DA, DB and DC are all radii, so triangles ABD and ACD are isosceles and their base angles match the marked ones: \(\angle DAB = \angle DBA = 19^\circ\) and \(\angle DAC = \angle DCA = 19^\circ\). That makes the inscribed angle \(\angle BAC = 38^\circ\), and a central angle is twice the inscribed angle on the same arc, so \(\angle BDC = 76^\circ\). In radians that is \(\frac{76\pi}{180} = \frac{19\pi}{45}\), and in lowest terms \(a + b = 19 + 45 = 64\).
note: DEFECT: the printed stem is only the last sentence — everything else is in the figure, and the figure never states that D is the centre of the circle, which is required to fix the answer. Figure: circle with A on the top arc, B lower left and C lower right on the circle, D marked inside at the centre; segments AB, AC, DB, DC are drawn and the angles ABD and ACD are each marked 19 degrees. Answer 64 assumes D is the centre; without that statement the angle is not determined.

stem: A regular hexagonal prism has a volume of 350 cubic inches and a height of 14 inches. What is the perimeter of each of the hexagonal bases, in inches? Round your answer to the nearest tenth of an inch.
whyCorrect: The base area is \(\frac{350}{14} = 25\) square inches. A regular hexagon of side s has area \(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}s^2\), so \(s^2 = \frac{50}{3\sqrt{3}} = \frac{50\sqrt{3}}{9}\) and \(s = \frac{5\sqrt{2}\,\sqrt[4]{3}}{3}\). The perimeter is \(6s = 10\sqrt{2}\,\sqrt[4]{3} = 10\sqrt[4]{12} \approx 18.6\) inches.

whyWrong.B: \(10\sqrt{3} \approx 17.3\) comes from \(s^2 = \frac{25}{3}\) — dividing the area by 3 but dropping the \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) in the hexagon formula.
whyWrong.C: This treats the base as a square: \(s^2 = 25\) gives \(s = 5\) and a perimeter of 30. A hexagon of area 25 has a shorter side than that.
whyWrong.D: \(25\sqrt{3} \approx 43.3\) multiplies by \(\sqrt{3}\) where the formula divides by it, giving a hexagon more than five times too big in area.

note: The book prints choice D as "25 \u221a3 66"; the trailing 66 is the page number.

stem:
For triangles PQR and KLM, the angles Q and L are equivalent and \(PR = \frac{3}{4}KM\). Which of the following information is enough to claim that PQR and KLM are similar?
I. The length of PQ is \(\frac{3}{4}\) of the length of KL.
II. The length of LM is \(\frac{3}{4}\) of the length of QR.
whyCorrect: Angle Q sits between QP and QR, while PR is the side opposite it. Statement I adds PQ, so you have an angle plus one adjacent side plus the opposite side — that is SSA, which does not fix a triangle's shape (e.g. \(\angle Q = 30^\circ\), \(PQ = 10\), \(PR = 6\) allows \(QR \approx 11.98\) or \(QR \approx 5.34\), and KLM may take either shape scaled up). Statement II runs the ratio the wrong way: the given \(PR = \frac{3}{4}KM\) makes PQR the smaller triangle, but \(LM = \frac{3}{4}QR\) makes KLM the smaller one, so it actually rules similarity out. Neither statement establishes it.

whyWrong.A: Statement I is the ambiguous SSA case — the equal angle is not between the two sides whose ratio you know, so two differently shaped triangles satisfy it.
whyWrong.B: Adding II makes things worse, not better: its ratio contradicts the given \(PR = \frac{3}{4}KM\), so the two statements together describe triangles that cannot be similar.
whyWrong.C: Statement II alone gives \(\frac{LM}{QR} = \frac{3}{4}\) while the stem gives \(\frac{PR}{KM} = \frac{3}{4}\); those point in opposite directions, so no common scale factor exists.

note: Disagreement with the obvious 'consistent ratio' reading is likely: statement I looks sufficient until you notice the known angle is not included between the two known sides. Question 96 in the same book turns on exactly this SSA point.

stem: A circle with radius of 8 cm is inscribed in an equilateral triangle. If the length of the triangle is \(k\sqrt{3}\) cm, what is the value of k?
whyCorrect: For an equilateral triangle of side s, the inscribed circle's radius is the apothem, \(r = \frac{s}{2\sqrt{3}}\). Setting \(8 = \frac{s}{2\sqrt{3}}\) gives \(s = 16\sqrt{3}\), so \(k = 16\). A common slip is using the circumradius formula \(r = \frac{s}{\sqrt{3}}\), which is the distance to a vertex, not to a side.
note: "The length of the triangle" is loose wording; it is read here as the side length. If it meant the perimeter the value would be 48.

stem: Right triangle ABC is inscribed in a circle with angle B = 90 degrees, BC > AB, and AC is a diameter of the circle. BD is perpendicular to AC with point D on AC. AC = 113 and \(BD = \sqrt{222}\). What is the ratio of CD/AD?
whyCorrect: The altitude to the hypotenuse satisfies \(BD^2 = AD \cdot DC\), so \(AD \cdot DC = 222\), and \(AD + DC = AC = 113\). Those two facts make AD and DC the roots of \(t^2 - 113t + 222 = 0\), which factor to \(t = 2\) and \(t = 111\). Because \(BC > AB\), the longer piece is on C's side, so \(DC = 111\), \(AD = 2\), and the ratio is \(\frac{111}{2}\).

whyWrong.B: This is \(\frac{AD}{CD}\) — the ratio upside down. The condition \(BC > AB\) is what tells you 111 goes with C.
whyWrong.C: This mixes the altitude into the ratio. \(\sqrt{222}\) is BD; the ratio asked for involves only the two pieces of the hypotenuse.
whyWrong.D: 111 is the length CD itself, not the ratio \(\frac{CD}{AD}\); dividing by \(AD = 2\) is still required.

stem: A triangular pyramid with edge length 48 has a surface area equal to \(k\sqrt{3}\). Find the value of k.
whyCorrect: All four faces of a regular triangular pyramid are equilateral triangles of side 48. One face has area \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(48)^2 = 576\sqrt{3}\), and the surface area counts all four: \(4(576\sqrt{3}) = 2304\sqrt{3}\), so \(k = 2304\). Counting only the three lateral faces (giving 1,728) is the usual mistake — the base is a face too.

stem: A right square pyramid has a surface area of \(64 + 16\sqrt{357}\) square inches, which includes a base area of 64 square inches. What is the height, in inches, of this pyramid?
whyCorrect: The base area of 64 gives a base edge of 8. Subtracting it leaves \(16\sqrt{357}\) for the four triangular faces, and each face has area \(\frac{1}{2}(8)(\ell) = 4\ell\), so \(16\ell = 16\sqrt{357}\) and the slant height is \(\ell = \sqrt{357}\). The height, slant height and half the base edge form a right triangle: \(h = \sqrt{357 - 4^2} = \sqrt{341} \approx 18.47\). Using the full edge 8 instead of the apothem 4 is the usual error.
note: The exact height is \u221a341 \u2248 18.4662, so both 18.46 and 18.47 should be accepted; the book's numbers do not produce a whole-number height.

stem: A circle in the xy-plane has its center at \((-3, 3)\). Line t is tangent to this circle at the point \((6, -3)\). Which of the following points also lies on line t?
whyCorrect: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. The radius from \((-3,3)\) to \((6,-3)\) has slope \(\frac{-3-3}{6-(-3)} = -\frac{2}{3}\), so line t has slope \(\frac{3}{2}\). Through \((6,-3)\) that is \(y = \frac{3}{2}x - 12\), and \(x = 12\) gives \(y = 6\).

whyWrong.A: The tangent line crosses the y-axis at \(y = -12\), not \(\frac{5}{2}\); this point is nowhere near line t.
whyWrong.B: \((3,12)\) is another point on the circle — its distance from the center is \(\sqrt{117}\), the same as the radius. A tangent touches the circle only at \((6,-3)\).
whyWrong.D: This lies on the line of slope \(\frac{2}{3}\) through \((6,-3)\): the sign was flipped without taking the reciprocal. The perpendicular slope to \(-\frac{2}{3}\) is \(\frac{3}{2}\).

stem: To determine if age and gender are related to pet ownership at his school, Mark selected a random sample of 50 male 14- to 15-year-old students from the school and a random sample of 60 female 17- to 18-year-old students from the school. For each student, he recorded the student's age, gender, and whether the student owned a pet. Which of the following provides the best explanation for why Mark cannot draw a valid conclusion from this study?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The sample sizes are too small.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The two samples are not of equal size.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Mark will be unable to tell whether a difference in pet ownership is related to age because the two age groups are too close in age.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Mark will be unable to tell whether a difference in pet ownership is related to gender because of the difference in age. Similarly, he will be unable to tell whether a difference in pet ownership is related to age.

whyCorrect: Every male in the study is 14-15 and every female is 17-18, so gender and age change together across the two groups. When two variables move in lockstep like this they are confounded: any difference in pet ownership could be caused by either one, and no analysis of these data can separate them.

whyWrong.A: 50 and 60 are perfectly workable sample sizes; the study fails no matter how many students are added, because the design itself ties gender to age.
whyWrong.B: Comparison groups do not have to be the same size. Unequal sizes affect precision slightly, not the validity of the conclusion.
whyWrong.C: 14-15 and 17-18 are distinct age bands, not "too close." And the problem is not the size of the age gap — it is that the age gap coincides exactly with the gender split.

stem:
A science class studied the feeding behavior of the birds that visited a bird feeder each school day for a period of time. The table summarizes the number of birds the class observed visiting the bird feeder each school day during this period of time.
Number of birdsNumber of days
143
153
164
171
183
199
What is the median number of birds the class observed visiting the bird feeder each school day during this period of time?
whyCorrect: The second column counts days, so there are \(3+3+4+1+3+9 = 23\) days and the median is the 12th value in order. Running totals: 3 days at 14, 6 through 15, 10 through 16, 11 through 17, 14 through 18. The 12th day falls in the 18-bird group, so the median is 18. Taking the middle row of the table (16 or 17) is the trap — the rows are not equally weighted.

stem: A researcher surveyed undergraduate students, graduate students, and postgraduate students. The number of undergraduate students surveyed was 7450% of the number of postdoctoral students surveyed and the number of graduate students surveyed was 24% of the undergraduate students surveyed. If there were 3576 graduate students surveyed, what was the sum of the number of undergraduate students and postdoctoral students surveyed?
whyCorrect: Work backwards from the graduate count. Graduates are 24% of undergraduates, so undergraduates \(= \frac{3576}{0.24} = 14{,}900\). Undergraduates are 7450% of postdoctoral students, and 7450% means 74.5 times, so postdoctoral \(= \frac{14{,}900}{74.5} = 200\). The sum is \(14{,}900 + 200 = 15{,}100\).
note: The stem introduces "postgraduate" students but then asks about "postdoctoral" students; the two are used for the same group.

stem: Each of the three data sets represented by the three dot plots has 18 values. The median of data sets A, B, and C are a, b, and c respectively. What is the relationship between a, b, and c?
whyCorrect: With 18 values, each median is the average of the 9th and 10th values. Counting up from the left in each plot, the 9th and 10th dots all land on 5 in all three data sets, so \(a = b = c = 5\). The plots differ in spread — A has a stray value at 9, C is spread across 1 through 9 — but spread does not move the middle.

whyWrong.A: This reads the widths of the plots rather than their centers. C is the most spread out, but its middle two values are still 5.
whyWrong.B: Same error in reverse: A's long right tail at 9 pulls the mean up, not the median.
whyWrong.C: There is no ordering at all here; all three middles coincide.

stem: The dot plot represents 13 values in data set A. Data set B is created by adding 39 to each of the values in data set A. Which of the following correctly compares the median and standard deviations of data sets A and B?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The median of data set B is equal to the median of data set A, and the standard deviation of data set B is equal to the standard deviation of data set A.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The median of data set B is greater than the median of data set A, and the standard deviation of data set B is equal to the standard deviation of data set A.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The median of data set B is greater than the median of data set A, and the standard deviation of data set B is greater than the standard deviation of data set A.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The median of data set B is less than the median of data set A, and the standard deviation of data set B is equal to the standard deviation of data set A.

whyCorrect: Adding the same number to every value slides the whole distribution 39 units to the right. Every measure of center moves with it, so the median goes up by 39. Standard deviation measures how far values sit from their mean, and those distances are unchanged by a shift, so it stays the same.

whyWrong.A: The median does change — every value, including the middle one, is 39 larger.
whyWrong.C: Standard deviation would only grow if the values spread out from one another. Adding a constant moves them together, keeping every gap identical.
whyWrong.D: Adding a positive number cannot lower the median.

note: Dot plot for data set A (13 values): 33 appears 4 times, 34 three times, 35 three times, 36 twice, 37 once. The plot is not actually needed to answer the question.

stem: The positive number a is 2,800% of the number c, and c is 20% of the number b. What is the value of \(a - b\) in terms of c?
whyCorrect: 2,800% means 28 times, so \(a = 28c\). The second relationship runs the other way: c is 20% of b, so \(c = 0.2b\) and therefore \(b = 5c\). Then \(a - b = 28c - 5c = 23c\).

whyWrong.B: This treats b as 20% of c instead of the reverse, and then multiplies rather than subtracts somewhere: \(28 \times 5 = 140\).
whyWrong.C: \(560c\) is \(28 \times 20c\) — it uses 20 as a multiplier instead of converting 20% to \(\frac{1}{5}\), and multiplies instead of subtracting.
whyWrong.D: \(2{,}240c\) comes from multiplying the two percentages as whole numbers (2,800% of 20% written as \(28 \times 80\)); the question asks for a difference.

stem: A researcher selected 26 guinea pigs from one habitat and 18 wild cavies from another habitat at random in Venezuela. The researcher found that in early adolescence, the number of virtual squares the wild cavies crossed was significantly more than the number of virtual squares the guinea pigs crossed. The researcher also found that the number of virtual squares crossed by both the wild cavies and the guinea pigs decreased from early adolescence to late adolescence. Based on the researcher's findings, which of the following statements is an appropriate conclusion that can be drawn from this study?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The statistically significant difference in behavior between the two age groups was caused by the differences in habitat.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The statistically significant difference in behavior between the two age groups was caused by aging.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The statistically significant difference in behavior during early adolescence between the two groups of animals can be generalized to all guinea pigs and wild cavies.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The statistically significant difference in behavior during early adolescence between the two groups of animals can only be generalized to the habitats in the study.

whyCorrect: The animals were selected at random from two particular habitats, not randomly assigned to conditions. Random selection lets you generalize to the populations sampled — the animals in those two habitats — and nothing wider; the lack of random assignment means no cause can be claimed at all.

whyWrong.A: This claims a cause. Species and habitat vary together here, so the study cannot separate them, and an observational study cannot establish causation in any case.
whyWrong.B: Also a causal claim, and the same objection applies: nothing was manipulated, so aging is only one of several possible explanations.
whyWrong.C: Too wide. The sample came from two specific habitats in Venezuela, so it supports conclusions about those populations, not about every guinea pig and wild cavy.

whyCorrect: Standard deviation measures how far the values sit from the mean, so look for the table whose frequencies pile up hardest on a single value. In A, 55 of the 75 values are exactly 7 and the rest are only one unit away, giving a standard deviation of about 0.52. Every other table spreads its counts across all five values, so all of them are wider.

whyWrong.B: This is a mound shape but a wide one — 22 of its 75 values sit two units from the center, giving a standard deviation of about 1.28.
whyWrong.C: Its frequencies are nearly flat (15, 15, 15, 18, 15), so the values at 5 and 9 are as common as the middle ones; the standard deviation is about 1.40.
whyWrong.D: This is the widest of the four, not the narrowest: the counts are largest at the two extremes 5 and 9 and smallest in the middle, giving about 1.51.

stem: Researchers must conduct an experiment to see whether a new vaccine is effective in relieving certain allergies. They have selected a random sample of 100 patients suffering from allergies. Some of the patients are assigned to the new vaccine while the rest are assigned to the traditional treatment. Which of the following methods of assigning each patient's treatment is most likely to lead to a reliable conclusion about the effectiveness of the new vaccine?

choices.label: A
choices.content: Those who have more than one allergy are assigned to the new vaccine.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The median weight of the patients is found. Those who weigh less than the median weight are assigned to the new vaccine.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The patients divide themselves evenly into two groups. A coin is tossed to decide which group is assigned to the new vaccine.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Each patient is given a random number. Those with an even number are assigned to the new vaccine.

whyCorrect: The point of assignment is to make the two treatment groups alike in every respect except the treatment. Only D assigns each individual patient by chance, so severity, weight, age and everything else you did not think to measure end up spread evenly between the groups. Any later difference can then be attributed to the vaccine.

whyWrong.A: This puts every more-severe case in the vaccine group. If the vaccine then looks worse, you cannot tell whether that is the vaccine or the severity.
whyWrong.B: Splitting on weight builds a systematic difference into the groups, so weight and treatment are confounded from the start.
whyWrong.C: The coin only decides which group gets the vaccine; the groups themselves were formed by the patients choosing whom to stand with, so friends, severity and habits cluster together.
